title: LangGraph: streaming, multi-agent, the 11-node copilot
seriesDescription: LCEL, tools, retrievers, tracing, StateGraph, reducers, checkpointers, human-in-the-loop and streaming. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Stream modes and what they emit, supervisor and subgraph patterns (and their reducer trap), Send fan-out, and drawing the 11-node copilot graph from memory.
source: LangGraph docs (streaming, subgraphs, multi-agent, get_stream_writer); LangChain docs; verified by running langgraph 1.2

questions.prompt: Parent and subgraph share the key `x` declared as `Annotated[list, operator.add]`. The parent node `p1` returns `{'x': ['p1']}`, then the subgraph node `sub` `runs;` inside, node `s1` returns `{'x': ['s1']}`. The parent started with `x = []`. How many items are in `x` at the end?
questions.explanation: The subgraph receives x = `['p1']`, appends 's1' and returns its full state `['p1', 's1']`; the parent's add reducer then appends that to `['p1']`, giving `['p1', 'p1', 's1']`: 3 items. I ran it. Fix by giving the subgraph its own state schema or an overwrite/dedupe reducer.

questions.prompt: Reference design used in this roadmap, an 11-node copilot graph: `guard_in` (input policy check, no LLM), router (LLM classifier), retrieve (vector search), `grade_docs` (LLM relevance check), `tool_agent` (LLM with `bind_tools`), tools (`ToolNode`), approval (human interrupt), `sql_gen` (LLM text-to-SQL), `sql_validate` (code check), `sql_exec` (read-only run), respond (LLM answer, streamed). A tool question takes exactly one tool round with no approval: `guard_in`, router, `tool_agent`, tools, `tool_agent`, respond. How many LLM calls does it make?
questions.explanation: LLM nodes on that path: router (1), `tool_agent` twice (2 and 3: one to request the tool and one after the result) and respond (4). `guard_in`, tools are not LLM nodes. Count LLM calls to estimate cost and latency per path.

questions.prompt: Reference design used in this roadmap, an 11-node copilot graph: `guard_in` (input policy check, no LLM), `router` (LLM classifier), `retrieve` (vector search), `grade_docs` (LLM relevance check), `tool_agent` (LLM with `bind_tools`), `tools` (`ToolNode`), `approval` (human interrupt), `sql_gen` (LLM text-to-SQL), `sql_validate` (code check), `sql_exec` (read-only run), `respond` (LLM answer, streamed). A data question generates SQL, and `sql_validate` rejects the first two attempts and routes back to `sql_gen` `each time;` the third attempt passes and executes. How many LLM calls are made in total?
questions.explanation: router (1) + `sql_gen` three times (3) + respond (1) = 5. `sql_validate` and `sql_exec` are plain code. Cap the regeneration loop with a counter in state so a stubborn failure does not run forever.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: A subgraph that shares an `operator.add` list key with its parent can make entries appear twice in the parent state.
questions.reason: The subgraph returns its whole state for the shared key, and the parent's reducer appends it to what the parent already holds.

whys.a: Right: input entries come back in the subgraph output and the reducer appends them again; I reproduced it by running.
whys.b: R is the cause of A, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Options: transform state at the boundary (call the subgraph inside a node and return only new items), use a separate schema in the subgraph, or use an id-based reducer like `add_messages`.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: `stream_mode`='values' emits the full state after every step, so its payload grows as the state grows.
questions.reason: `stream_mode`='updates' emits only the changes that each node returned, keyed by node name.

whys.a: R is a fact about a different mode, so it does not explain A.
whys.b: Both are true: they are two modes with different payloads; neither explains the other.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Use updates for progress UIs and logs, values when the client needs the whole state each time, messages for token streaming.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: In the supervisor pattern, the supervisor node can pick the next worker with `Command(goto=worker_name)`.
questions.reason: Workers can never hand control back to the supervisor once they have run.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: A is true; R is false: workers normally return to the supervisor, which decides the next step or finishes. I ran such a loop.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: The supervisor pattern is a loop: supervisor -> worker -> supervisor ... -> END. Handoff-style swarms let agents pass control directly to each other instead.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: `stream_mode='messages'` emits one item each time a node finishes.
questions.reason: `stream_mode='messages'` emits LLM token chunks together with metadata such as `langgraph_node`.

whys.a: A is false, so a is wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is false: per-node-completion is the updates mode; R is true and describes messages mode, which I confirmed by running.

questions.explanation: In messages mode you receive `(message_chunk, metadata)` tuples; filter on `metadata['langgraph_node']` to show only the final answer node, not router or SQL generation tokens.

questions.prompt: Match each `stream_mode` value with what it emits.

right.text: Per-node state changes, keyed by node name
Data your nodes emit themselves through a stream writer
Detailed execution events: tasks and checkpoints
Only the final answer, once the run is complete

questions.explanation: Passing a list of modes returns (mode, chunk) tuples. The final output alone is simply `invoke()`.

questions.prompt: Match each node of the 11-node copilot graph with its responsibility.

right.text: Rejects prompt injection or out-of-policy input before any LLM spend
Judges whether retrieved chunks are relevant to the question
Checks the generated SQL is one read-only statement on allowed tables
Pauses with `interrupt()` until a human approves a risky action
Executes the tool calls requested by the model (`ToolNode`)

questions.explanation: The other nodes: router (classifies the intent), retrieve (vector search), `tool_agent` (LLM with bound tools), `sql_gen`, `sql_exec` (read-only execution with timeout) and respond (final answer, the node whose tokens you stream).

questions.prompt: Complete the wiring of the 11-node copilot graph.
questions.text: START goes to {1} first; sql_gen feeds {2}, which routes forward to sql_exec or back to sql_gen; tool_agent loops with {3} until the model stops requesting tools.
questions.explanation: Drawing it from memory: `guard_in` -> router -> {retrieve -> `grade_docs` | `tool_agent` <-> tools (via approval for risky calls) | `sql_gen` -> `sql_validate` -> `sql_exec`} -> respond -> END.

questions.text: Use stream_mode="{1}" to push LLM tokens to a chat UI, "{2}" to show which node just finished, and "{3}" when the client needs the whole state each step.
questions.explanation: You can combine modes in a list. For custom progress events use the custom mode with a stream writer.

questions.prompt: Stream tokens from the compiled graph app (inputs and cfg exist) in messages mode and print only the tokens produced by the node named respond, without newlines.
questions.explanation: `meta.get`('`langgraph_node`') works equally if you adapt the check by comparing to 'respond'; the regex also accepts the subscript form. Without the filter you would stream router and SQL-generation tokens to the user.

questions.prompt: Write a routing function `fan_out(state)` for `add_conditional_edges` that sends every item in `state['items']` to the node `'work'` in parallel, as a separate task whose input is `{'item': item}`.

checks.label: returns a list of Send objects

questions.model:
def fan_out(state):
    return [Send("work", {"item": it}) for it in state["items"]]
questions.explanation: This is LangGraph's map-reduce pattern; give the collected key a reducer such as `operator.add`. I ran an equivalent graph and each item was processed by its own task.

questions.prompt: A compiled graph `sql_sub` exists. Add it as a node named sql_agent to the builder g, wire START -> sql_agent -> END and compile it into app.
questions.model:
g.add_node("sql_agent", sql_sub)
g.add_edge(START, "sql_agent")
g.add_edge("sql_agent", END)
app = g.compile()
questions.explanation: A compiled graph is a runnable, so it can be a node directly when schemas share keys. Otherwise call `sql_sub`.invoke inside a wrapper function to map state in and out.

questions.prompt: Print the Mermaid diagram text of the compiled graph app, which is the quickest way to check the copilot wiring you drew from memory.
questions.explanation: `draw_mermaid_png`() renders an image. Declare destinations (Command return types or `add_node` destinations) so Command-routed edges show up in the picture.

questions.prompt: Reference design used in this roadmap, an 11-node copilot graph: `guard_in` (input policy check, no LLM), router (LLM classifier), retrieve (vector search), `grade_docs` (LLM relevance check), `tool_agent` (LLM with `bind_tools`), tools (`ToolNode`), approval (human interrupt), `sql_gen` (LLM text-to-SQL), `sql_validate` (code check), `sql_exec` (read-only run), respond (LLM answer, streamed). Where must the approval node sit for a risky write tool such as sending an email?

options.text: Between `tool_agent` and tools, so the call runs only after a human resumes the graph.
options.why: Right: the interrupt sits before the side effect, and the checkpointer keeps the pending call.

options.text: After tools, so the human can only reject the email once it has already been sent out.
options.why: Too late: the side effect has already happened.

options.text: Inside `guard_in`, which approves or rejects every user message before the graph even starts.
options.why: Approving messages is not approving actions; the dangerous call is generated later by the model.

options.text: After respond, so the person only approves the wording of the final answer text for the user.
options.why: The answer text is not the risky action; the tool execution is.

questions.explanation: Human approval gates the action, not the chat. Pair it with idempotent tools and an audit entry; the node restarts after resume, so avoid side effects before `interrupt()`.

questions.prompt: Inside a node `work(state)`, emit the custom progress event `{'progress': 'half'}` with LangGraph's stream writer and return no state change. Then show how the caller of the compiled graph `app` (variables `inputs` and `cfg` exist) receives only those custom events.
questions.explanation: `get_stream_writer()` returns a callable that pushes any payload into the custom stream (I ran it with `stream_mode=['custom','updates']` and got both). Use it for progress bars and long-running tool status, separate from token streaming.
